abstract: Degenerative eye diseases affect millions of people and can ultimately lead to blindness. Facilitating regeneration of retinal neurons in mammals could prevent or slow vision loss. Spiny mice (genus Acomys) display remarkable regenerative abilities across many tissues, including the spinal cord. Utilizing the neurotoxin NMDA to damage inner retinal neurons, we assessed the response to retinal damage in Acomys using the well documented response of Mus musculus as a baseline for comparison. In response to acute retinal damage, two waves of cell proliferation were detected in Acomys: the first wave (1-4 dpi) mostly consisted of proliferating microglia, whereas the second wave (6-21 dpi) included microglia and Muller glia. Reactive gliosis was significantly reduced in Acomys compared to Mus, with minimal expression of acute gliotic markers such as GFAP and NES after injury. In Acomys retinas, proliferating microglia of various activation states were observed weeks after injury, whereas in Mus, the microglia returned to a resting state by 10 dpi. Additionally, by 121 dpi, recovery of RBPMS+ ganglion cells was detected in Acomys, a small number of which were also positive for EdU, suggesting they were derived from proliferating cells. Taken together, our results show that the retinal damage response in Acomys features an initial burst of microglial proliferation, followed by some Muller glial proliferation, reduced reactive gliosis, and RGC recovery. As such, these findings create a novel opportunity to explore potential mechanisms of retinal repair and neural recovery in mammals.
